connector: Mama should have been home hours ago. At the very first light, Annemarie sees her on the ground at the edge of the meadow. In Chapter 13 everything depends on something small, and on who is left to carry it. In Chapter 14 a girl runs alone into the dark woods. Watch what she tells herself as she runs.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, this is Grete. Mama has come home hurt, and something important was left behind by the steps. This is the last week of the novel, and the last week of your essay. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapters 13 and 14, and write your conclusion. Today’s question: what does brave running look like when you don’t know exactly why you’re running?
transcripts.wgrd: This week, read like a detective with two boxes. One box holds what could really have happened in Denmark in 1943. The other holds what the author shaped to make a good story. Make your two columns. When you aren’t sure where something goes, write the question down. The Afterword, at the end of the week, will help you check.
transcripts.dol: The model is a short sentence about running through the woods. The sentence to fix has three words in it that sound almost alike. Decide whether each one is the right twin for its spot. Then find the place where one thought ends and the next one begins, and give each thought a capital.
transcripts.guide1: This week’s word work is about words that sound exactly alike. Say them out loud and you can’t tell them apart. Only the spelling shows which one the writer meant. Nobody gives you the rule first. Hunt for the twins, and work out for yourself how a reader is supposed to know.
transcripts.morphology: Have you ever seen a whole street of windows light up, one candle at a time? This week’s three roots are about shape and about bending, and every right word lights a candle in a window. Some words take the shape root, and some take a bending root. Before you choose, think about what the word is doing.
transcripts.vocabulary: Four words for the last week of the book. Two of them are about fitting a shape and bending back. Two are about the careful work you’ll do with the Afterword: putting two things side by side, and deciding at the end. Read each sentence, take the word apart, and make a guess before you flip.
transcripts.grammar: Read this sentence out loud and listen. Several words in it have a twin, a word that sounds exactly the same but is spelled differently and means something else. Tap every one. Then try to say the rule. If your ear can’t tell the twins apart, what can?
transcripts.spelling: Same hunt, different sentence. Your ear won’t help you here, so slow down and look. Which words have a sound-alike twin? Tap them. Then think about how you’ll remember which spelling goes with which meaning. Some people make up a little trick for each pair.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about being the one who is there. When I was ten, our neighbor fell on the stairs, and her baby was crying alone upstairs. No grown-up was home. I wasn’t brave, only nearest, so I went up. Annemarie isn’t the oldest or the strongest. She is the one who can go. Watch what she decides.
transcripts.read: Chapter 13 starts at dawn, with Mama on the ground at the edge of the meadow. Watch what Annemarie finds near the steps, and who decides what to do about it. Then, on the path in Chapter 14, listen to the story Annemarie tells herself as she runs. Why that story, on this path?
transcripts.copia: Here is one plain sentence: Annemarie ran toward the path. Say it three new ways. Give it a new beginning, swap in a stronger running word, and add a detail about how she ran. The sentence keeps its bones. But each version shows a slightly different girl running into the woods.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. The questions ask what Mama tells Annemarie to do, and why, and then for one small detail that shows Annemarie is scared and keeps going anyway. The last one asks you to hold this scene up against the real history from Week 15. Then you write your essay’s conclusion.
transcripts.chapter: The third question is the week’s big one. Lowry gives us one girl on one path. The real rescue had hundreds of people, on many paths and many boats. Find one way this scene is like what really happened, and one way it’s different. Both answers can be true at once.
transcripts.workshop: Today you write the ending of your essay. A good conclusion doesn’t just say, the end. It says your claim again in fresh words, names how your character changed, and then looks forward, out of the book and into the real world. Three moves. Sam shows you how first. Then you try.

a.raw: their parents told them to walk to the bend in the path they’re going there now
a.fixed: Their parents told them to walk to the bend in the path. They’re going there now.
a.why: A capital T to start; their is right (it shows belonging). A period ends the first thought. They’re (they are) is right too, and it starts a new sentence, so it needs a capital. A period at the end.

b.raw: mama and annemarie packed their basket they’re hoping it gets there in time
b.fixed: Mama and Annemarie packed their basket. They’re hoping it gets there in time.
b.why: Capitals on the names Mama and Annemarie. Their (belonging) and there (a place) are both the right twins. A period ends the first thought, and They’re (they are) starts the second with a capital. A period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain why Mama trusts Annemarie with it.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain which matters more to the story, the fear or the going on.
scholar.journal-q3: … and explain why Lowry might have told this part of history through one girl.

match.conform: Conform has the shape root inside it. Look for the meaning about matching or fitting in.
match.reflect: Reflect has a bending root inside it. Look for the meaning about bending back, or thinking back.
match.compare: Compare is about putting two things side by side. Look for the meaning about what is the same and what is different.
match.conclude: Conclude is about the end. Look for the meaning about finishing, or coming to a final idea.

eg: With the basket on her arm, Annemarie ran toward the path.
Annemarie ran toward the path, as fast as she could.

wordgame.h: Four windows on a dark street
wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Ask what each word is about: a shape, or bending?

why.t: On the evening of May 4, 1945, Danish radio from London told Denmark that the German soldiers there were giving up. For five years, every window had been covered at night so that no light could show. That evening, people tore down the dark curtains, and light shone from the windows again. A few years later, Danes began putting candles in their windows every May 4 to remember, and many still do. form means shape, and flect and flex both mean bend. Each right word lights one window. Four each lesson, until the whole street glows.

miss.fill1: Not quite. Read the meaning again. Is this word about a shape, or about bending?
miss.fill2: Not quite. Read the meaning again. Is this word about a shape, or about bending?
miss.fill3: Not quite. This word is about bending, not a shape. flect and flex both mean bend, so say the word out loud and listen to its ending.
miss.fill4: Not quite. This word is about bending, not a shape. flect and flex both mean bend, so say the word out loud and listen to its ending.

wordgame.winDay: Four candles are burning on the dark street. The next lesson’s words light more windows.

notes.wgrd: Historical fiction mixes real history with made-up scenes. Sort what could be real from what was shaped for the story, and save your questions for the Afterword.
vocab: To match a shape or rule; to fit in with something.
To think back; or, to bounce light or an image.
To look at two things and notice what is the same and what is different.
To finish; to come to a final idea.
notes.wordParts: form means “shape,” and flect and flex both mean “to bend”: conform, reform, reflect, flexible.
notes.grammar: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings and spellings: their (belonging), there (a place), they’re (they are); to (toward), too (very or also), two (the number).
notes.spelling: Your ear can’t tell homophones apart, so look at each one and ask what it means in that spot. The meaning decides the spelling: to the water, too dangerous, two soldiers.

case.title: Little Red Riding-Hood
case.alt: A painting of a little girl in a red hood sitting up in bed beside a wolf dressed in a white bonnet.
label: Gustave Doré was a French artist who drew and painted pictures for old fairy tales. In this painting, the wolf has dressed up as Grandmother, and Little Red Riding-Hood is only beginning to understand.
In Chapter 14, Annemarie tells herself this story as she runs the dark path to the boat, the way she once told it to Kirsti. A story she knows by heart gives her mind something steady to hold.

look.q: Why might a story you know by heart help when you are scared?
look.a: You know how it goes and how it ends, so it gives your mind something steady to hold on to.

look.q: How is Annemarie’s path like Little Red Riding-Hood’s, and how is it different?
look.a: Both walk alone through woods with a basket for someone. But Annemarie’s danger is real soldiers, not a wolf in a story.

case.credit: Gustave Doré, Little Red Riding Hood, oil painting, about 1862. Photo: Chris Olszewski, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
